plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Downs cell, the industrial electrolytic apparatus used to produce pure sodium metal from molten sodium chloride via the reaction 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The cell interior contains a bath of molten NaCl, with a cylindrical iron screen separating the electrode compartments; the cathode (−) occupies the outer annular region and the anode (+) projects upward from the bottom center, both connected to an external voltage source at the lower right. Liquid sodium metal, which is less dense than the molten salt, rises and collects in a side reservoir on the right, from which it drains through a labeled Na outlet; simultaneously, Cl2 gas produced at the anode rises through a central green-tinted collector tube and exits through a labeled Cl2 outlet at the upper right, while fresh NaCl is fed continuously through an inlet at the top. The iron screen physically segregates the two products — liquid sodium and gaseous chlorine — preventing their recombination and enabling continuous, separate collection of each. This figure demonstrates the Downs cell as the industrial-scale process for sodium production and explains why aqueous electrolysis cannot substitute for it, since H+ ions are more easily reduced than Na+ ions at any cathode in contact with water.

interactions.label: Run electrolysis
interactions.teaches: Current drives Cl− ions to the central anode where Cl2 gas bubbles up and out, while Na+ ions migrate through the screen to the outer cathode where liquid sodium forms, rises, and drains to the Na outlet — the screen keeps the two products apart

interactions.label: Inspect electrodes
interactions.teaches: Each electrode hosts one half-reaction: oxidation 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e− at the anode (+), reduction Na+ + e− → Na at the cathode (−), and clicking either region reveals its balanced half-equation and which product it makes

demo_steps.title: Cell anatomy
demo_steps.narration: Molten NaCl fills the cell. A central anode sits inside a cylindrical iron screen, with the cathode outside it; both connect to the voltage source. Note the two separate exits — Cl2 at top, liquid Na at the side.

demo_steps.title: Run the current
demo_steps.narration: With current flowing, Cl− ions drift to the anode and Cl2 gas rises through the green collector; Na+ ions move outward to the cathode and form liquid sodium, which — being less dense than the melt — floats up into the side reservoir.

demo_steps.title: Half-reactions
demo_steps.narration: Click each electrode: the anode oxidizes chloride (2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−) and the cathode reduces sodium ions (Na+ + e− → Na). Together they sum to 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The iron screen and the density difference are the whole design: they physically segregate freshly formed Na and Cl2 so the products of electrolysis never meet and recombine into NaCl — which is also why the electrolyte must be molten, not aqueous (water would be reduced instead of Na+).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Vertical cross-section, symmetric layout. Gray outer tank filled with pale blue-purple molten NaCl up to a visible liquid line. Center: salmon-colored anode rod rising from the floor, ringed by a hatched-mesh iron screen cylinder; dark cathode plates flank the screen on both sides, wired (with the anode) to a gray 'Voltage source' box at lower right. Above the anode, a pale-green hood narrows into a tall pipe bending right to the labeled 'Cl2 outlet' with an arrow; small yellow-green bubbles animate upward inside it. Top center: a small valve labeled 'Inlet for NaCl'. Right side: a pink-shaded reservoir arm collecting 'Liquid Na metal' draining to the labeled 'Na outlet'. During animation, show small '+'-marked Na ions drifting outward toward the cathode and '−'-marked Cl ions drifting inward toward the anode, with bubbles rising and the pink Na level slowly filling. Clicking the anode region highlights it and pops a callout with '2Cl− → Cl2(g) + 2e− (oxidation)'; clicking the cathode region shows 'Na+ + e− → Na(l) (reduction)'. Labels in plain sans-serif as in the original textbook figure.

authoredContext:
The most important method for the production of sodium is the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride; the set-up is a Downs cell , shown in . The reaction involved in this process is:

Separation of the molten sodium and chlorine prevents recombination. The liquid sodium, which is less dense than molten sodium chloride, floats to the surface and flows into a collector. The gaseous chlorine goes to storage tanks. Chlorine is also a valuable product.

Pure sodium metal is isolated by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using a Downs cell. It is not possible to isolate sodium by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of sodium salts because hydrogen ions are more easily reduced than are sodium ions; as a result, hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of the desired sodium metal. The high temperature required to melt NaCl means that liquid sodium metal forms.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram is a T-shaped structure labeled, “Anode ( positive sign ),” that is on a mesh-like background labeled, “Iron screen.” The anode is connected to a box labeled, “Voltage source,” by a line, and the voltage source is connected to one of two L-shaped structures that surround the anode. They are labeled, “Cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the cathode on the right side of the diagram is a tube connected to a collection chamber labeled, “N a metal,” that has a lower outlet labeled, “N a outlet.” Surrounding all of these components is a blue background labeled, “Molten N a C l,” and a series of tubes that form a square outside the diagram. They have an opening in the upper right corner labeled, “Inlet for N a C l.” At the top of the diagram is a large tube with an upward-facing arrow drawn on it. The tube turns right, has a right-facing arrow on it, and is labeled, “C l subscript 2 outlet.”

discrepancies: the iron screen is drawn as a flat rectangular grid, while the source shows a cylindrical mesh with a visibly curved front face wrapping around the anode
the green collector hood is much wider and boxier than the source's narrow tapered funnel with an upward arrow inside it; the rising-gas arrow inside the hood is missing

the source's rectangular anode is a copper-colored block connected directly through the tank floor; the generated version adds an extra narrow stem below the block and places it lower, partially overlapping the wire routing
the Na collection pipe in the source exits through the bath wall as a channel; the generated figure uses a free-floating pink flask beside the tank that does not connect into the cell interior
the 'Iron screen' and 'Molten NaCl' leader lines point near the anode/bath edge rather than clearly at the mesh and bath surface as in the source
evaluation.notes: Clearly recognizable as the Downs cell for NaCl electrolysis with correct electrode polarity, separate Cl2/Na exits, and strong, functional interactions (animated ion drift, bubbling, Na reservoir fill, electrode half-reaction popups, step player); main weaknesses are the flat rectangular screen instead of a curved cylindrical mesh and a disconnected flask-shaped Na reservoir.
action_items: Redraw the iron screen with a curved bottom edge and slight perspective curve on the vertical mesh lines so it reads as a cylinder enclosing the anode, as in the source.
Narrow and taper the green collector hood and add the upward arrow inside it indicating rising Cl2 gas.
Connect the pink Na reservoir to the cell wall with a short channel so liquid sodium visibly flows from the bath into the side collector.
Adjust the 'Iron screen' leader line so it terminates on the mesh itself rather than beside the anode block.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interactivity are excellent (5/5), but there are concrete execution-level geometry and labeling fixes — curved cylindrical screen, tapered hood with gas arrow, connected Na reservoir channel, and corrected leader lines — all addressable by the generator without changing the plan.
